ECE 1100 DISCOVERY PROJECT · IN PROGRESS

Arduino Reaction Time Game

A physical interface for measuring a human response.

The problem & motivation

Reaction time looks simple: a light appears, someone presses a button, and the elapsed time is recorded. But measuring that action accurately requires a physical system whose inputs, outputs, and timing logic work together. I chose this project because it makes the relationship between hardware and software tangible. Instead of interacting with an abstract program on a screen, the player responds to a real LED and button while a microcontroller manages the rules.

Planned architecture

The proposed build uses an Arduino Uno, breadboard, LED, 220-ohm resistor, push button, jumper wires, and a USB cable. The Arduino will wait through a randomized delay before turning on the LED. Once the LED activates, the player presses the button; the program will calculate the interval between those two events and report the reaction time in milliseconds. A crucial design requirement is false-start detection: if the button is pressed before the LED appears, the system must reject that attempt rather than treating it as a valid result.

Engineering process

The project connects microcontroller programming, digital input and output, randomized scheduling, elapsed-time calculations, basic circuit design, and human-computer interaction. My planned process begins with gathering parts and assembling the circuit, then writing and testing the Arduino logic one behavior at a time. I will verify that the LED is triggered after a variable delay, that button presses are read consistently, and that the reported time corresponds to the event sequence. I also plan to test premature presses and repeat trials to identify inconsistent wiring, debounce issues, or timing bugs.

Current status & next steps

This feature is intentionally documented as in progress: it is based on my original project pitch, not a claim that the final hardware has been completed or demonstrated. Before the Discovery Project Showcase, I will add authentic photos of my assembled circuit, implementation details, observed results, challenges, and a reflection on what changed during testing. The Hive in Georgia Tech’s Interdisciplinary Design Commons is a planned resource for parts, breadboarding, and assembly assistance. This page will become the record of that iterative process.

From a strong

My long-term goal is to become a software engineer working on challenging, large-scale systems. I am especially interested in backend and infrastructure-oriented roles involving distributed services, performance optimization, cloud technologies, and developer platforms. I also want to explore how AI can make existing infrastructure easier to understand, operate, and improve.

While I’m completing my Computer Engineering degree, I’ll keep building the fundamentals that make ambitious systems possible: algorithms, computer architecture, software design, mathematics, and practical engineering judgment.
